newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. says Afghan crop good, but food aid needed.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Afghan crop good, but food aid needed.

text.p: Afghanistan is expected to produce its biggest harvest in 18 years of warfare this year, but will still need 170,000 tons of emergency food aid for some 1.75 million people in the coming months, a U.N. statement said.

The statement, issued in Islamabad, said the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) had estimated 1997 cereal output at 3.66 million tonnes, 18 percent higher than last year's 3.1 million tonnes.
This year's harvest, the biggest since 1978, includes 2.71 million tonnes of wheat, 400,000 tonnes of rice, 300,000 tonnes of maize and 250,000 tonnes of barley, the statement said.

It quoted a joint report by the FAO and WFP as saying that improved security in southern areas, sufficient rains and relatively little pest damage favoured agricultural production, but that fighting in the north could disrupt harvesting.

"The eight northern provinces are forecast to produce 1.3 million tonnes of cereals from the current harvest, but if the intensity of military activities increases or the conflict widens over the next few months, harvesting could be interrupted, and a reduction from this forecast is possible," the report said.
Even if the favourable forecast holds, Afghanistan will need to import some 710,000 tonnes of cereals, mainly for an urban population swollen by the return of refugees, it said.

It estimated that Afghanistan will need 170,000 tonnes of emergency food aid, including 150,000 tonnes of cereals, for the 1997-1998 marketing year. WFP is expected to supply 140,000 tonnes, and non-governmental organisations the remainder.
The aid will be distributed to the most vulnerable Afghans, including internally displaced persons, returnees, households headed by women, the sick and the elderly, the statement said.

There has been heavy fighting in some parts of northern Afghanistan in recent weeks, particularly in the fertile Shomali Valley just north of Kabul, where opposition fighters have been battling the purist Islamic Taleban militia.
The mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban control Kabul and about two thirds of Afghanistan but have failed to quell opposition forces drawn mainly from ethnic minorities in the north.
